ev.justification: Rec. (1) establishes the strategic sectors of the Union industry. The European Industrial Maritime Strategy (EIMS), published with the IAA on 4.3.26, explicitly recognises the maritime manufacturing industry as a strategic sector for the EU’s autonomy, resilience, defence, economic security and decarbonisation. Omitting the maritime industry would create an inconsistency between  IAA and EIMS. Its inclusion ensures coherence between the instruments signalling that the Eu maritime value chain has the same strategic recognition as other industries and the automotive.

European production is particularly strong in high-performance and specialised textile applications, where manufacturing capacity, know-how and reliability are key. ev.amended: (1c)In some Member States, existing nickel, ferronickel and cobalt production and processing facilities remain suspended, such as LARCO in Greece, with a serious impact on jobs. The expansion of the company's activities to include electricity production, based on proposals submitted by workers' unions, can contribute to addressing energy poverty. Reopening it with environmental upgrading and the use of new methods such as electrolysis and hydrometallurgy, which enable the exploitation of ‘poor’ minerals, will contribute to the employment of a significant number of workers and the exploitation of the country's existing energy and mineral wealth, which remains unexploited due to tough international competition despite the significant increase in the prices of these minerals.

(1c)Regulation (EU) 2024/1252 of the European Parliament and of the Council establishes a framework for ensuring a secure and sustainable supply of critical raw materials. That objective is inextricably linked to this Regulation, given that the re-industrialisation of Europe, the decarbonisation of strategic sectors, the development of clean technologies, and the production of batteries, industrial components, energy equipment and essential goods all require stable, secure and, as a matter of priority, European access to critical raw materials, as well as a reduction in excessive reliance on third countries.

(3a)Circularity and resource efficiency are essential components of a resilient and competitive industrial base. Keeping materials, components and products in use at their highest value reduces the Union's dependence on imported primary raw materials, lowers exposure to supply disruptions and price volatility, and can reduces the energy and emissions embedded in industrial production. The objectives of this Regulation should therefore support the circularity and resource efficiency of the Union's manufacturing sector alongside its decarbonisation and resilience, in line with the Union's climate-neutrality objective set out in Regulation (EU) 2021/1119. Circularity projects are projects that contribute to make available secondary raw materials, products or components intended to substitute primary raw materials or newly manufactured products or components in the supply chains of energy intensive industries, net-zero technologies and automotive industry.

(3a)Measures that raise the price of steel, concrete, aluminium, vehicles or energy fall on citizens and taxpayers. No requirement under this Regulation should apply unless it is shown not to increase the cost of living or the cost of doing business.

(3b)The electrification of the Union’s economy is a central driver of its decarbonisation, energy security and industrial competitiveness. This Regulation therefore supports the electrification of strategic sectors, namely the electrification of the automotive sector, the decarbonisation of energy-intensive industries, including through the direct use of electricity in industrial processes, and the manufacturing of net-zero technologies that enable it. Furthermore, the Action Plan for Affordable Energy indicates that every person, community and business should benefit from the clean transition, and identifies investments in modernising and expanding the electricity network as essential to facilitate the deployment of renewables, electrification and new industrial and business demand. While the Union electrification rate was only 23,4 % in 2024, the Clean Industrial Deal and the Affordable Energy Action Plan introduced a key performance indicator on the share of electricity in final energy consumption, setting 32 % by 2030 as reference. The Commission Communication of 22 April 2026 entitled “AccelerateEU - Energy Union” identifies accelerating electrification as an urgent measure to end the Union's exposure to fossil fuel price shocks and import dependencies, and announces the introduction of an indicative Union-wide electrification target of 46 % by 2040 in the Commission Communication of 17 July 2026 entitled “Electrification Action Plan”.

(7a)Renewable energy generation, battery storage, electricity grids and the electrification of industrial processes are strategic assets for the competitiveness, resilience and energy security of the Union. Measures under this Regulation should therefore be implemented in a manner that accelerates the deployment of renewable generation, storage, grid infrastructure and renewable electricity sourcing.
ev.justification: Manufacturing capacity is essential, but it depends on a strong and affordable domestic market for renewable electricity and flexibility assets.

ev.justification: The current wording of recital (9) limits the scope of the provision to electric vehicles and electric vehicle components, thereby excluding a significant portion of the automotive value chain that is equally exposed to competitive pressures from third countries and strategic dependencies. The amendment seeks to broaden the reference to encompass all vehicles and vehicle components, while preserving the specific mention of electric powertrain-related technologies in view of their particular relevance to the Union's decarbonisation objectives. This broader framing better reflects the actual risk landscape facing the Union automotive industry as a whole, and ensures that the protective and resilience-oriented measures envisaged by this Regulation are not confined to a single vehicle technology segment. In this context, the acceptance of the principle of technological neutrality - including vehicles powered exclusively by renewable fuels (so-called VEEFs) - is a prerequisite for Italy to advance in the negotiation of the IAA.

The Commission's impact assessment ranks them third among the automotive components most exposed to imports: imports from third countries rose from EUR 881 million in 2010 to EUR 1 360 million in 2024, and the share of Chinese tyres from 29% to 58%.

ev.original: (9)The automotive industry is a cornerstone of the Union economy. With a view to delivering on the Union’s climate policy objectives, over the past years, the European automotive industry has been investing heavily in the development of cleaner vehicles and innovative components. Electric vehicles and electric vehicle components, including traction batteries, e-powertrain components and electronic systems, are essential technologies for advancing the decarbonisation of road transport. However, as a result of costs disadvantage and the transformation of the value chain with an increasing value share for batteries, e-powertrain and electronics, the level of Union content in vehicles produced in the Union is decreasing. It is no longer possible to postpone effective measures to avoid the risk of local production being displaced. In the absence of such measures, the current circumstances would lead to a full reliance on third countries for key vehicle components. That would be a serious threat to the Union’s economic security and future resilience, as well as for its climate goals.
ev.amended: (9)The automotive industry is a cornerstone of the Union economy. With a view to delivering on the Union’s climate policy objectives, over the past years, the European automotive industry has been forced to invest heavily in the development of cleaner vehicles and innovative components. Electric vehicles and electric vehicle components, including traction batteries, e-powertrain components and electronic systems, are essential technologies for advancing the decarbonisation of road transport. However, as a result of wrong policies, costs disadvantage and the transformation of the value chain with an increasing value share for batteries, e-powertrain and electronics, the level of Union content in vehicles produced in the Union is decreasing. It is no longer possible to postpone effective measures to avoid the risk of local production being displaced. In the absence of such measures, the current circumstances would lead to a full reliance on third countries for key vehicle components. That would be a serious threat to the Union’s economic security and future resilience.

(9a)The maritime manufacturing industry, encompassing shipbuilding, ship repair, maintenance, conversion, recycling and the full maritime equipment supply chain, constitutes a cornerstone of the Union's industrial base for the Union’s decarbonisation efforts and the achievement of its climate targets. Key technologies for decarbonisation of the maritime sectors need specific protection in particular for shipbuilding, green ferries, specialised vessels and short sea shipping. In line with the Commission’s port and maritime industrial strategies (COM(2026) 111 final and COM(2026) 112 final), the sector has been investing in cleaner vessels, low- and zero-emission fuels, wind propulsion and energy-efficient and digital technologies, which are essential to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from maritime transport. However, the global shipbuilding market is characterised by strong state-backed and distortive competition from third countries, competitors benefiting from public financing schemes, systematic local content requirements and coordinated industrial policies. These measures place European shipbuilders and maritime equipment manufacturers at a structural competitive disadvantage. Without sufficient shipbuilding activity in Europe, equipment manufacturers will gradually lose industrial capacity, innovation capabilities, decarbonisation capacity, and skilled workforce, weakening the resilience of the entire European maritime value chain. In the absence of such measures, the Union would face growing dependencies on third countries for critical maritime technologies, undermining its resilience and its ability to meet climate objectives.

(9a)Activities relating to the recovery of materials produce secondary raw materials that are used both upstream and downstream across the value chains of the energy-intensive industries, of the automotive sector and of net-zero technologies, as well as in the wider industrial ecosystems. Recycled steel scrap contributes directly to the decarbonisation of the Union's steel industry, recycled aluminium is essential to the aluminium value chain, and recycled critical raw materials play a growing role in the manufacturing of batteries, motors and net-zero technology components. Activities relating to the recovery of materials are therefore of strategic importance for the resilience of Union industrial supply chains, for the achievement of the Union's circular economy objectives, for the reduction of industrial greenhouse gas emissions, decreasing critical dependencies and strengthening he overall economic security of the Union. The definition of low-carbon products under this Regulation should fully recognise the contribution of recycled materials to decarbonisation objectives, including through taking into accounted the avoidance of greenhouse gas emissions associated with the use of secondary raw materials in production processes.

(9b)The textile industry and its whole value chain constitute a strategic pillar of the Union's industrial base and an industrial sector which still needs to decarbonise itself. In 2022, out of 12 categories of European household consumption, textile consumption ranked, on average, the fifth largest in terms of environmental and climate pressures. In 2023, the EU textile and clothing sector had a turnover of EUR 170 billion, employing about 1.3 million people across 197,000 companies. EU textiles production mainly specialises in technical textiles (such as. non-wovens, technical and industrial textiles, ropes and fabrics for use in healthcare and agriculture, sportswear, etc.) and in high-value clothing and footwear. The infrastructure, construction and car sectors rely on textile as a material and there is a strong share of the sector that goes through public procurement. Yet, the textile market is characterised by strong state-backed and distortive competition from third countries, whose competitors benefit from public financing schemes and coordinated industrial policies. The European Commission estimates that around 4.6 billion low-value parcels entered the EU in 2024, about 12 million per day. More than 90 % of them were from China, a significant share of which comprises T&C items, underscoring the scale of direct-to-consumer imports that bypass traditional retail and customs channels. This, with other unfair practices, place EU textile producers at risk, with weekly ongoing factory closures. The pandemic has revealed how strategic the sector could be, with the shortage of face masks. This is why developing EU local content requirements for the textile sector, combined with other instruments, has the potential to stop the ongoing deindustrialisation process, allow the decarbonisation of the sector and protect EU strategic autonomy.

ev.original: (15)The Union should adopt a more strategic approach in leveraging its economic weight and the value of access to its internal market. In that context, the strategic use of public intervention is essential to prevent critical dependencies in the Union. Public procurement amounts to 15% of the Union’s GDP. Contracting authorities and entities should therefore, where appropriate, ensure that public procurement requirements foster economic security and resilience of supply chains. Public support schemes also play an important role in stimulating demand in downstream sectors that account for a significant share of demand for certain strategic products and technologies. Such schemes should therefore favour beneficiaries that make a greater contribution to strengthening the Union’s resilience and advancing its decarbonisation objectives. Auctions are crucial for the deployment of net-zero technologies and should be designed to foster demand for such technologies including components originating from the Union.
ev.amended: (15)The Union should adopt a more strategic approach in leveraging its economic weight and the value of access to its internal market. In that context, the strategic use of public intervention is essential to prevent critical dependencies in the Union. Public procurement amounts to 15% of the Union’s GDP. Contracting authorities and entities should therefore, where appropriate, ensure that public procurement requirements foster economic security and resilience of supply chains. Public support schemes also play an important role in stimulating demand in downstream sectors that account for a significant share of demand for certain strategic products and technologies. Such schemes should therefore favour beneficiaries that make a greater contribution to strengthening the Union’s resilience and advancing its decarbonisation objectives. To ensure the effectiveness of these provisions, the definition of auction should also cover capacity mechanisms exclusively targeting the deployment of net-zero technologies, in particular battery energy storage systems, which represent a growing share of the Union's deployment of strategic storage capacity but currently fall outside the scope of the auction framework.

(15a)Within the vehicle value chain, certain components, notably tyres, are critical throughout a vehicle's life. Through their rolling resistance, tyres can account for up to 30% of the energy needed to move a vehicle, which affects CO2 emissions from conventional vehicles and electricity consumption in electric vehicles, whatever their technology or age. Taking tyre performance, as shown by the fuel efficiency and wet grip classes under Regulation (EU) 2020/740, into account in public procurement and support schemes would advance the Union's climate, competitiveness and road-safety objectives, while supporting an industry facing intense competition from third-country imports. Tyres should therefore be recognised as a strategic product of the vehicle value chain.
ev.justification: Tyres can account for up to 30% of the energy needed to move a vehicle and can influence emergency braking distances by 20–30%. Best-performing tyres that can be identified through the EU tyre label, cut CO2 emissions from combustion vehicles, extend the range of electric vehicles and improve road safety. As tyres are replaced several times over a vehicle's life, they sustain European production and employment long after the vehicle leaves the factory.

ev.amended: (15a)Within the vehicle value chain, certain components—notably tyres—are critical throughout a vehicle's lifecycle. By reducing rolling resistance, tyres can account for up to 30% of the energy needed to move a vehicle, cutting CO2 emissions from conventional vehicles and electricity consumption in electric vehicles. Considering tyre performance in public procurement and support schemes would advance the Union's climate, competitiveness and road-safety objectives while supporting an industry facing intense competition from non-EU imports. Tyres should therefore be recognised as a strategic product of the vehicle value chain.
ev.justification: The IAA should include product-performance requirements in procurement and support schemes. Tyres are a key example: although only 2–3% of vehicle value, they influence 20–30% of energy efficiency and can reduce emergency braking distances by 20–30%. Existing EU tyre labelling already measures these criteria, enabling use without new administrative burdens. Supporting high-performing tyres would strengthen decarbonisation, road safety, EU competitiveness and resilience, given their broad economic and strategic importance.

ev.amended: (19)Demand-side measures should focus on establishing low-carbon requirements, requirements relating to the use of sustainable carbon sources, or both for steel, cement and aluminium used in buildings, infrastructure and motor vehicles, as well as fertilisers, selected plastic applications and selected chemicals through measures targeting relevant end markets, where appropriate, since those sectors are the most energy-intensive industries. The measures should also take into consideration products end-of-life characteristics, such as biodegradability and compostability of plastics. Targeted Union wide demand-side measures can help create lead markets for low-carbon and Union-produced energy-intensive industrial products, supporting decarbonisation while strengthening the Union’s industrial base, provided that adequate supply-side support measures, in particular related to competitive energy costs, are in place to enable Union producers to effectively respond to and benefit from such market opportunities.
ev.justification: This amendment clarifies that demand-side measures may include requirements relating to the use of sustainable carbon sources in addition to low-carbon requirements for plastics and chemicals. This is particularly relevant for the chemical sector, where the transition depends both on lower-emission production processes and on the progressive substitution of fossil carbon feedstocks with recycled, bio-based and carbon capture and utilisation sources. The amendment also broadens the reference to energy-intensive sectors by including chemicals, plastics and fertilisers, reflecting their role in industrial value chains and their relevance for the low-carbon and circular transition. It further clarifies that demand-side measures should be accompanied by adequate supply-side conditions enabling Union producers to respond to the demand created. By linking demand-side requirements with enabling conditions on the supply side, the provision improves the feasibility and impact of lead market measures. It also reduces the risk of unmet demand being fulfilled primarily by imports, due to a lack of EU supply competitiveness, thereby supporting the objective of strengthening the Union’s industrial base. This improves the coherence of the Regulation with its objectives of creating lead markets, supporting the industrial low-carbon and circular transition and strengthening the Union’s industrial base.

ev.amended: (20a)The replacement market accounts for about three quarters of tyre sales in the Union. It is the main channel through which public demand can support tyre manufacturing in the Union and the segment most exposed to imports. Rubber products for motor vehicles, including tyres, hoses and belts supplied as replacement parts, should therefore be subject to the low-carbon and Union origin requirements. For truck and bus tyres public demand should also favour tyres retreaded in the Union, which use far less material and cause considerably lower emissions than new tyres.
ev.justification: Three quarters of EU tyre sales are replacement tyres, the segment most exposed to imports. Public procurement and support should therefore also cover rubber products bought as replacement parts. Retreading truck and bus tyres preserve the casing and roughly halves cradle-to-gate emissions compared with a new tyre.

(23a)In order to ensure legal certainty and protect investments made in zero-emission vehicles in accordance with the existing Union regulatory framework, including Directive 2009/33/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council1a, the application of new Union origin requirements should provide for an appropriate transition period and should not affect vehicles registered in the Union before the application of those requirements. Such vehicles should therefore remain eligible for use for the remainder of their normal operational lifetime.

1a Directive 2009/33/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 April 2009 on the promotion of clean and energy-efficient road transport vehicles
ev.justification: Public transport operators and authorities have made substantial long-term investments in zero-emission vehicles under existing Union legislation and policy frameworks, including Directive 2009/33/EC. Legal and investment certainty requires both an appropriate transition to the new Union origin requirements and the protection of investments already made.Given the long operational lifetime of buses and coaches, a fixed end date for vehicles already registered in the Union could result in the premature stranding or replacement of functioning zero-emission vehicles. At the same time, equivalent transition periods should apply to direct vehicle procurement and service-based procurement to ensure a coherent application of the new requirements.

ev.amended: (24a)Member States should design public support schemes, in a way that they contribute to the objectives of strengthening the Union’s strategic industrial value chains through the Union-origin requirements and low-carbon content requirements, as well as compliance with applicable social and labour law. When designing such public support schemes, Member States should design public support schemes in a manner that discourages the relocation of manufacturing activities supported outside the territory of the Union. To provide legal certainty and ensure the effective use of public funds, where such relocation nevertheless takes place within five years from the date on which the support is granted, or within three years in the case of SMEs, the support granted should be recovered by the competent authority. Member States should apply these requirements to public support schemes accounting for at least 90% of the total national budget allocated to schemes that benefit households or companies and that primarily aim to support the construction or renovation of buildings for residential and commercial purposes and infrastructure and the lease and purchase of motor vehicles for civil purposes, and accounting for 100% of the total national budget allocated to other forms of public intervention and financial support for corporate vehicles.

(24a)Member States should design public support schemes in a manner that contributes to the objectives of strengthening the Union’s strategic industrial value chains through Union-origin requirements and low-carbon content requirements, ensuring compliance with applicable social and labour law, and discouraging the relocation outside the territory of the Union of supported manufacturing activities. To provide legal certainty and ensure the effective use of public funds, where such relocation nevertheless takes place, within five years from the date on which the support is granted, or within three years in the case of SMEs, the support granted should be recovered by the competent authority. Member States should apply these requirements to public support schemes accounting for 100% of the total national budget allocated to schemes that benefit households or companies and that primarily aim to support the construction or renovation of buildings for residential and commercial purposes and infrastructure and the lease and purchase of motor vehicles for civil purposes, and accounting for 100% of the total national budget allocated to other forms of public intervention and financial support for corporate vehicles.
ev.justification: Public support should provide a clear and predictable demand signal for low-carbon and Union-origin products. The co-rapporteurs propose increasing from 45% to 90% the share of the national budget allocated to the public support schemes covered by Part II of Annex II to which these requirements apply. This amendment increases that share to 100%, so that the requirements apply to the entirety of the relevant support budget. This approach is justified, as public support schemes covered by Part II of Annex II already represent a targeted segment of the market. Applying the requirements to the entirety of the relevant support budget would maximise the leverage of public expenditure in creating lead markets for low-carbon and Union-origin products, without extending the requirements to the wider market. The targeted derogations already provided for in this Regulation ensure sufficient flexibility where compliance would result in disproportionate costs or significant delays, making an additional general exemption for part of the national budget unnecessary. It is also consistent with the treatment of public procurement, where the requirements apply in principle to all procurement procedures falling within the scope of this Regulation, subject to targeted derogations. By contrast, auctions are subject to a differentiated coverage requirement, reflecting their role in supporting the rapid deployment of net-zero technologies.

ev.amended: (24a)Member States should apply Union-origin and low carbon requirements to all public support schemes benefitting households or companies, which primarily aim to support the construction or renovation of buildings or infrastructure for residential and commercial purposes, as well as for the lease and purchase of motor vehicles for civil purposes, and all other forms of public intervention and financial support for corporate vehicles. Member States should design public support schemes in a way that they contribute to the objectives of strengthening the Union’s strategic industrial value chains, as well as compliance with applicable social and labour law. When designing such public support schemes, Member States should ensure that the relocation of supported manufacturing activities outside the territory of the Union is discouraged. To provide legal certainty and ensure the effective use of public funds, where such relocation nevertheless takes place within five years from the date on which the support is granted, or within three years in the case of SMEs, the support granted should be recovered by the competent authority.

(24a)In order to ensure legal certainty and protect investments made in zero-emission vehicles in accordance with the existing Union regulatory framework, including Directive 2009/33/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council 41, the application of new Union origin requirements should provide for an appropriate transition period and should not affect vehicles registered in the Union before the application of those requirements. Such vehicles should therefore remain eligible for use without being subsequently affected by the new Union origin requirements.
ev.justification: Public transport operators and authorities have made substantial long-term investments in zero-emission vehicles under existing Union legislation. Legal certainty requires an appropriate transition to new Union origin requirements and protection of existing investments. Given buses’ long operational lifetime, a fixed end date could lead to premature replacement of functioning vehicles. Equivalent transition periods should apply to direct vehicle and service-based procurement.

ev.amended: (25a)For the purposes of calculating the EU-origin content in vehicles and vehicle components, components manufactured by the vehicle manufacturer or within its group should be assessed on the same basis as components that have been purchased, namely their full cost of production, established on the basis of audited cost accounting and, for intra-group transactions, on an arm’s length basis. The EU-origin value incorporated at any level of the supply chain, including into Tier 2 and Tier 3 components and into cast or forged parts, should be recognised where it is traceable, provided that the non-EU-origin value incorporated at any level is deducted on the same basis and provided that such tracing is applied to all the vehicle components rather than selectively. Profits, selling, marketing and general administrative expenses, as well as research and development carried out outside the Union, should not be accounted for as Union value.
ev.justification: Manufacturers themselves produce a large proportion of key components, which do not have an ex-works price. A single method for valuation is necessary to ensure that this European production is fully recognised. Symmetrical and non-selective tracing of EU value and non-EU value recognises Tiers 2 and 3, including forged parts, without artificially inflating EU-origin content.

ev.amended: (25a)Research and development is the foundation of the Union's capacity to innovate and to remain at the technological frontier in the automotive sector, in particular in batteries, electric powertrains and vehicle software. The location of research and development activities largely determines where future value, skills and intellectual property are created. Vehicle manufacturers that concentrate the bulk of their research and development effort in the Union contribute directly to the Union's technological sovereignty and to the anchoring of high-quality jobs. It is therefore appropriate to reward those manufacturers by granting them a bonus when calculating their share of compliant vehicles for the purposes of the fleet-level compliance mechanism.

(25a)Public transport operators, in particular in smaller and peripheral markets, have already made substantial investments in zero-emission vehicles in line with Union's decarbonisation objectives. Considering the long operational lifetimes of buses and coaches, the application of Union-origin requirements should not create stranded assets, undermine investment predictability, or slow the deployment of zero-emission mobility solutions.

(25b)The application of Union origin requirements should take into account market availability, operational realities and the need to ensure continuity and affordability of public transport services across the Union, including in geographically peripheral and smaller markets where the availability of compliant vehicles may remain limited.
ev.justification: The availability of vehicles complying with Union-origin requirements differs significantly across Member States and market segments. In smaller and geographically peripheral markets, limited supplier availability may reduce competition, increase procurement costs and delay fleet renewal. This amendment ensures that Union-origin requirements are applied in a manner that supports operational continuity, affordability and the continued decarbonisation of public transport services across the Union.

(27a)Batteries are a key technology for the decarbonisation of transport and for the Union's industrial autonomy. The security and resilience of their value chain depend heavily on access to a limited number of raw materials, in particular lithium, nickel, manganese and cobalt, which are classified as strategic raw materials under Regulation (EU) 2024/1252. In order to strengthen the Union's industrial sovereignty and reduce critical dependencies, the Union-origin requirements applicable to batteries used in vehicles covered by this Regulation and to battery energy storage systems covered by Regulation (EU) 2024/1735 should include a specific obligation that at least 20 % by mass of the strategic raw materials relevant to the battery concerned shall be mined, processed or recycled within the Union. This requirement should apply irrespective of the battery chemistry used, including nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) and lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) chemistries, in order to ensure a technology-neutral approach that supports both existing and emerging battery technologies in the Union.

(28a)In the Communication on an Industrial Action Plan for the European Automotive Sector published on 5 March 2025, the Commission announced conditions for inbound foreign investments in the automotive sector to further increase their added value for the EU. Such conditions could include joint venture requirements, senior management requirements, facilitating agreements that support the needs of EU industry, licensing of technology or intellectual property, commitments to supply critical inputs. Such announcement has created reasonable expectations for foreign investors, which may therefore lead to an acceleration of new or planned foreign investment projects in the Union before any conditions start applying. This could lead to a significant reduction of the effectiveness of the provisions on foreign investment contribution of this Regulation aiming at strengthening the resilience of supply chains and the Single Market. It is therefore necessary to start applying the conditions foreseen for foreign direct investments retroactively and starting from the date of publication of the Communication on an Industrial Action Plan for the European Automotive Sector.

ev.original: (29)In order to ensure that the internal market remains attractive for investment, and that investment adds value to the Union’s economy and society, it is necessary to establish common conditions for foreign direct investment in manufacturing emerging strategic sectors. Those sectors should be manufacturing sectors with innovative potential where Union entities are not at or near the global innovation frontier, and where appropriate Union capacities and participation should be ensured. Harmonised criteria should apply to foreign investors of a third country which holds over 40% of the global manufacturing capacity in emerging strategic sectors. To ensure the effectiveness of the provisions of this Regulation, the Commission should monitor the global manufacturing capacity of those sectors and publish the results.
ev.amended: (29)In order to ensure that the internal market remains attractive for investment, and that investment adds value to the Union’s economy and society, it is necessary to establish common conditions for foreign direct investment in manufacturing emerging strategic sectors. Those sectors should be manufacturing sectors with innovative potential and strategic relevance for the Union, and where Union entities are either not at or near the global innovation frontier, or where they are but this position is increasingly threatened, such that appropriate Union capacities and participation should be ensured. Strategic sectors in scope should be certain net-zero technologies as defined under the NZIA Regulation (battery technology, solar technology, on- and offshore wind technology, EV’s, hydrogen, heat pumps, hydropower and electric charging technologies) as well as critical raw materials. Harmonised and objective criteria should apply to foreign investors or their subsidiaries, in the Union or elsewhere, of a third country which holds over 40% of the global manufacturing capacity in emerging strategic sectors. To ensure the effectiveness of the provisions of this Regulation, the Commission should monitor the global manufacturing capacity of those sectors and publish the results.

(30a)Certain manufacturing sectors are of particular strategic importance for the Union’s economic security, resilience, technological capacity and clean energy transition and may therefore warrant particular consideration in the context of foreign direct investment. This is the case for emerging strategic sectors in which the development and scaling-up of Union manufacturing capacity is essential to reduce strategic dependencies and preserve technological and industrial capabilities, including battery technologies and their value chains, electric and fuel-cell vehicles and related components, solar technologies and hydrogen technologies, including electrolysers and fuel cells. Such consideration is also warranted for established strategic sectors where maintaining a strong and competitive Union manufacturing base is essential for the deployment of technologies necessary for the Union’s energy and climate objectives and for the resilience of related supply chains. This includes onshore and offshore wind technologies, for which the Union has developed significant manufacturing capabilities and specialised supply chains encompassing final products and key specific components.

(35a)Investment funds, in particular private equity funds, infrastructure funds and other vehicles managed by asset management companies, may play a significant role in the financing, restructuring, modernisation and development of the Union’s industrial undertakings. However, their contribution to the objectives of this Regulation depends on the chosen investment strategy and horizon. Particular attention should be paid to acquisitions primarily funded through debt, in particular leveraged buyouts, where the financial burden resulting from the acquisition is transferred directly or indirectly to the acquired undertaking, reducing its capacity to finance productive investments, research and development, modernisation and skills development. A distinction should be made in this connection between measures implemented on the basis of a genuine industrial strategy and those which primarily pursue a short-termist financial policy based on the accumulation of debt, a reduction in capital expenditure, the disposal of assets or cash distribution, which run the risk of permanently weakening the undertaking’s productive, technological and decision-making capacities. In particular, the pursuit of a financial return should not lead to a situation where the cost of the acquisition is passed on to the undertaking itself, or where efforts to safeguard high-quality jobs are undermined or the undertaking’s integration into the Union’s value chains and industrial areas is weakened. In sectors covered by this Regulation, scrutiny of such measures should therefore take into account the level and distribution of the debt taken on to finance the acquisition, the undertaking’s capacity to service this debt without reducing its productive investments, the planned holding horizon, the asset distribution and disposal policy as well as the existence of a credible industrial strategy for investment, modernisation, innovation, employment and skills development.

(35b)Investments by sovereign funds, public strategic investment funds and other investment vehicles held or controlled by third countries may serve as an important source of long-term capital for the Union’s economy. The sole fact that they are public should not therefore create a presumption against them. However, when vehicles of this kind are held, controlled, financed or managed by a third country of concern, or when they pursue not only financial objectives but also strategic, technological, industrial or trade policy objectives defined or coordinated by such a country, any investment in the Union’s strategic industrial assets, critical technology areas or production capacities should be subject to enhanced scrutiny. This should take into account their beneficial owner, their governance, their financing, the rights available to them, their relationship with the public authorities in the relevant third country and their ability to exercise effective control, whether directly or indirectly.

ev.original: (39)To minimise the risk of circumvention through fragmented or indirect acquisitions, where several foreign investors act in concert, or where investments are made through affiliated entities or complex ownership structures, their respective interests should be aggregated by the Investment Authority for the purpose of determining the investment value and the notification threshold. Aggregation should also apply to existing holdings in the same Union undertaking or asset, whether direct or indirect, individual or joint, to ensure that successive transactions leading to significant influence or control are duly notified.
ev.amended: (39)To minimise the risk of circumvention through fragmented or indirect acquisitions, where several foreign investors or foreign investors’ subsidiaries act in concert, or where investments are made through affiliated entities or complex ownership structures, their respective interests should be aggregated by the Investment Authority for the purpose of determining the investment value and the notification threshold. Aggregation should also apply to existing holdings in the same Union undertaking or asset, whether direct or indirect, individual or joint, to ensure that successive transactions leading to significant influence or control are duly notified. In particular, it should prevent a situation where a transaction forming an economic whole is artificially divided between multiple investors, vehicles or transactions in order to stay below the thresholds provided for by this Regulation.

ev.original: (55)To enable an adequate supply of critical raw materials for projects in the acceleration areas, the European Critical Raw Materials Board established by Article 35 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1252 should provide a platform to exchange information on critical raw materials related supply chain bottlenecks in the acceleration areas. It should be possible for projects in relevant areas to benefit from the Joint purchasing mechanism established in Article 25 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1252 to aggregate their demand for strategic raw materials and increase their negotiating power with potential sellers, especially when they contain small or medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and small mid-cap companies (SMCs).
ev.amended: (55)To enable an adequate supply of critical raw materials for projects in the acceleration areas, the European Critical Raw Materials Board established by Article 35 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1252 should provide a platform to exchange information on critical raw materials related supply chain bottlenecks in the acceleration areas. It should be possible for projects in relevant areas to benefit from the Joint purchasing mechanism established in Article 25 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1252 to aggregate their demand for strategic raw materials and increase their negotiating power with potential sellers, especially when they contain small or medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and small mid-cap companies (SMCs). The development of the Union’s strategic industrial capacity should also be underpinned by the collection, sorting, preparation and recycling of secondary raw materials of European origin, as well as their reintegration into European industrial value chains, particularly those derived from industrial waste, construction and demolition waste, batteries, electrical and electronic equipment, end-of-life vehicles and other waste streams containing critical or strategic raw materials. The recycling of these materials cannot be a substitute for maintaining and developing European extraction, processing, production and refining capacities, but it is an essential complement to reducing strategic dependencies, limiting imported emissions and securing supplies to the industrial sectors covered by this Regulation, in particular steel, aluminium, cement, batteries, clean energy technologies and nuclear technologies.

ev.justification: The draft IAA Regulation applies a single approach—European preference rules based on NZIA components—to all industrial value chains covered by the text, despite their diversity (automotive, renewables, nuclear fission, hydrogen, batteries, etc.). ev.original: (68)In line with the same policy objective pursued for renewable energy auctions under Regulation (EU) 2024/1735, this Regulation should extend the additional Union origin requirements to renewable energy auctions for certain renewable energy technologies, in order to contribute to strengthening the Union’s industrial base and ensuring resilience of net-zero technology supply chains. To reflect the specific characteristics of renewable energy auctions, the additional requirements should apply to the net-zero technologies that are most relevant in the context of auctions, which are battery energy storage systems, solar photovoltaic technologies, electrolysers, as well as on- and offshore wind technologies. Where Union origin requirements apply to auctions, other provisions setting similar requirements for public support schemes should not apply to those auctions.

(69b)Batteries play a pivotal role in the Union’s decarbonisation and industrial competitiveness. They are a key enabler of electric vehicles, stationary energy storage systems, grid flexibility and a wide range of industrial and consumer applications. In the case of batteries, the Union’s resilience therefore depends on the upstream stages of the value chain, namely precursors, cathode active materials and anode active materials, and on essential components. Global production of those materials is highly concentrated in a very small number of third countries, which creates a critical dependency and exposes Union battery manufacturers to supply disruption and coercion. Union-origin requirements should therefore address precursors, cathode active materials and anode active materials, in order to de-risk investment in Union battery manufacturing and to make the Union’s industrial base credible. Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 of the European Parliament and of the Council introduces minimum recycled content requirements for batteries from 2031. To make that obligation workable, the Union should be able to retain end-of-life batteries and the materials recovered from them within the Union and to recycle them there, while allowing recycled content to be used in Union-made batteries. Those materials are strategic and should be preserved in the Union. Circularity should therefore be at the core of the requirements applicable to batteries under this Regulation.

(69c)Lithium should be subject to specific provisions under this Regulation, in view of its particular position in the battery value chain. It is present in all battery chemistries, and the market for lithium depends to a very large extent on demand from batteries. In addition, a pipeline of lithium projects exists in the Union. In order to provide the stable and predictable framework needed to bring those projects to fruition, and to reduce the Union’s dependency on third-country supply, at least 20% of the lithium contained in batteries should have been extracted, processed or recycled in the Union.

ev.original: (70)Businesses and households are an essential part of the demand for net-zero technologies in the Union. Public support schemes designed to support consumer demand for such products are important tools for strengthening the Union’s economic security and accelerating the green transition. In order to build on the provisions of Regulation (EU) 2024/1735 on resilience, it is necessary to complement those provisions introducing additional requirements for battery energy storage systems, solar photovoltaic technologies and heat pumps. Such additional requirements should ensure that certain main specific components and, in some cases, the whole final product, originate in the Union. That approach is in line with the general objective of support schemes to promote socially-desirable outcomes, in view of making progress on the ambitions of the European Pillar of Social Rights as well as environmental and climate objectives. Furthermore, it should ensure sufficient diversification while strengthening strategic manufacturing capacity and technological sovereignty within the Union. Public authorities in charge of support schemes should have the possibility either to condition the eligibility of the scheme to the fulfilment of the requirements, or to grant additional financial compensation when the requirements are fulfilled. In the latter case, the additional financial compensation should have an incentivising effect. However, if State aid is involved, the additional financial compensation should not exceed the applicable maximum aid intensity.

Furthermore, it should ensure sufficient diversification while strengthening strategic manufacturing capacity and technological sovereignty within the Union. Public authorities in charge of support schemes should have the possibility either to condition the eligibility of the scheme to the fulfilment of the requirements, or to grant additional financial compensation when the requirements are fulfilled. In the latter case, the additional financial compensation should have an incentivising effect. Public authorities in charge of support schemes should have the option, where possible and proportionate, to give priority to granting additional financial compensation where the requirements are met, rather than systematically making eligibility for the scheme conditional on compliance with those requirements. The implementation of these requirements should take into account the actual availability of products and components originating in the Union, their impact on prices for end consumers, and the need to ensure that the technologies in question remain affordable for households, small and medium-sized enterprises, and businesses facing cost constraints. These requirements should not have the effect of unduly delaying access to the equipment needed for decarbonisation, nor should they exacerbate energy poverty or increase the financial burden on households and businesses.

ev.justification: Low-income households depend on subsidies to replace old heating devices, insulate homes or buy clean vehicles. (71a)The resilience of the Union's energy system depends not only on the cybersecurity of information and communication technologies but also on the security and operational control of equipment capable of directly controlling, converting, regulating, switching or interrupting energy or power flows. Power electronic equipment, battery management systems, energy management systems and other digitally controlled energy equipment may, individually or through coordinated or aggregated operation, materially affect the security, stability or continuity of the energy system. Appropriate safeguards should therefore ensure that no manufacturer, supplier or other third party retains unilateral technical control capable of materially affecting the operation of such equipment.
ev.justification: Digitally controlled energy equipment can directly affect physical energy flows. Cybersecurity requirements should therefore address not only ICT systems but also equipment whose operation may have a material impact on the energy system.

ev.original: (75)In line with the measures for public procurement, auctions and public support schemes, this Regulation should also complement Regulation (EU) 2024/1735 with Union origin requirements for Member State support to the construction of nuclear power plants and to the manufacturing of hydrogen electrolysers. To secure long term Union sovereignty, energy security, and sector resilience, it is essential that the new nuclear plants, both large scale reactors and small modular reactors, prioritise as much as possible Union sourced technologies and components while maintaining the highest quality standards. Such strategy will not only boost domestic capabilities but also position the Union as a reliable, competitive player in the global nuclear market. However, in order to prevent risks related to technological lock-in, the Union origin requirements for nuclear power plants should only apply to new-builds, excluding refurbishments and lifetime extensions of existing nuclear power plants.
ev.amended: (75)In line with the measures for public procurement, auctions and public support schemes, this Regulation should also complement Regulation (EU) 2024/1735 with Union origin requirements for Member State support to the construction of nuclear power plants and to the manufacturing of hydrogen electrolysers. To secure long term Union sovereignty, energy security, and sector resilience, it is essential that the new nuclear plants, both large scale reactors and small modular reactors, prioritise as much as possible Union origin in the areas of intellectual property ownership of components, location of manufacturing and processing operations, employment of the local workforce, Gross Value Added in the EU, as well as the location of long-term maintenance and services contracts within the EU. These holistic “Made in EU” criteria, tailored by project, will support Union sourced technologies while maintaining the highest quality standards. Such strategy will not only boost domestic capabilities but also position the Union as a reliable, competitive player in the global nuclear market. However, in order to prevent risks related to technological lock-in, the Union origin requirements for nuclear power plants should only apply to new-builds, excluding refurbishments and lifetime extensions of existing nuclear power plants.
ev.justification: In relation to AM 1, the draft IAA Regulation applies a single approach—European preference rules based on NZIA components—to all industrial value chains covered by the text, despite their significant differences (automotive, renewables, nuclear fission, hydrogen, batteries, etc.).Such a uniform approach risks oversimplifying diverse industrial realities and does not sufficiently account for sector-specific characteristics, such as project complexity, contractual structures, available European workforce, the presence of local industrial players, IP ownership, global market positioning, and national regulatory frameworks. This is particularly relevant for large-scale energy infrastructure projects, which differ significantly from technologies designed for serial production.To better reflect European added value across sectors, an alternative to the component-based approach is therefore proposed: holistic “Made in EU” criteria, assessed and adapted on a project-by-project basis. These criteria could be based on a set of KPIs defined by Member States, which are directly involved in delivering large-scale projects. KPIs could cover both macroeconomic factors (e.g. value added to local GDP and European ownership of IP) and microeconomic factors (e.g. local workforce employed and the number of European companies involved in the project).

ev.original: 1.For the purposes of this Chapter, content of Union origin refers to content originating in the Union.
ev.amended: 1.For the purposes of this Chapter, Union origin requirements refers to content originating in the Union, or, where relevant, project-tailored holistic ‘Made in EU’ criteria.
ev.justification: As set out in AMs 1 and 2, the draft IAA Regulation applies a single approach—European preference rules based on NZIA components—to all industrial value chains covered by the text, despite their diversity (automotive, renewable energy, nuclear fission, hydrogen, batteries, etc.).Such a uniform approach risks oversimplifying different industrial realities and does not sufficiently reflect sector-specific characteristics or the complexity of large-scale energy infrastructure projects, which differ significantly from technologies designed for serial production. For such projects, holistic “Made in EU” criteria could instead be assessed and adapted on a project-by-project basis to better capture their contribution to the European economy. These criteria could be based on a set of macro- and microeconomic KPIs, to be further defined in the proposed Regulation and selected by the Member States, which are directly involved in delivering such large-scale projects. This amendment therefore seeks to establish the possibility of using project-specific “Made in EU” criteria as an alternative to the NZIA component-based approach, where appropriate for specific technologies.

ev.amended: 1a.For the purpose of the Union origin requirements for vehicles laid down in this Chapter and in the Annex III, also a vehicle assembled in the United Kingdom shall be deemed assembled within the Union and the content originating in the United Kingdom shall be deemed to be content of Union origin.

1c.By way of derogation for the purposes of this Regulation, lithium extracted in a third country may be treated as equivalent to content of Union origin where that third country is party to a comprehensive free trade agreement with the Union which provides for specific commitments concerning critical or strategic raw materials and contributes to the security and diversification of the Union’s supply of such raw materials.
The Commission shall establish and regularly update the list of third countries fulfilling the conditions for the treatment of lithium as equivalent to content of Union origin laid down in the third subparagraph.

2a.By way of derogation for aluminium products, origin shall be determined based on the country where aluminium is first produced in liquid form via electrolysis and subsequently cast into its first solid form (smelt & cast rule). For the secondary production route, origin shall be determined based on the country of smelt for the primary input and the country of most recent cast for the scrap input.
ev.justification: For steel, the current definition using Regulation (EU) No 2013/952 cannot apply, as its ‘last substantial transformation’ rule would undermine the objective by allowing third-country steel to gain Union origin status through minor downstream processing. Such a loophole would risk diverting decarbonisation investments away from Europe and rewarding imports of partly finished products instead of supporting genuine EU -based production. A steel melt and pour requirement is necessary as an additional criterion in Article 7 to ensure that the objectives of the IAA are being met i.e. growing industry within the EU, securing EU resilience, strategic autonomy, economic security and public order. In particular, the Union Origin definition of Article 7 is relevant in the context of the Low-Carbon Steel Credit made in the EU under the CO2 standards of cars and vans. Therefore, it is about strengthening the automotive value-chain in the EU. Referencing the “melt and pour” definition adopted in Regulation EU 2025/0726 ensures regulatory coherence. Article 7a
Anti-circumvention of Union origin
1. Content originating from partner countries shall not be considered to be of Union origin, where circumvention exists. Circumvention exists where either of the following applies:
(a) the content is produced by an economic operator owned or controlled by a natural or legal person from a third country which holds more than 40% of global manufacturing capacity in the sector concerned;
(b) more than 50% of the value of the parts of the product originates in a third country which holds more than 40% of global manufacturing capacity in the sector concerned.
Ownership and control shall be assessed at the level of the beneficial owner at the end of the ownership chain, including where exercised indirectly through any person or undertaking acting on behalf of or at the direction of that owner. Control shall be presumed where such persons hold, individually or collectively, 25% or more of the share capital or voting rights of the operator concerned, or of the assets used to produce the content.
2. An economic operator offering content as equivalent to Union origin shall carry out a self-assessment to determine whether the content is subject to circumvention. On that basis it shall submit a self-declaration. The Commission shall adopt implementing acts laying down the standard form of that declaration, in accordance with the examination procedure referred to in Article 31(2).
3. Where circumvention by an economic operator is established on a second or any subsequent occasion within three years, that economic operator and any undertaking controlled by the same beneficial owner shall be excluded from any procedure or support covered by this Regulation for a period of between one and three years.
ev.justification: Partner content must not become a back door around the origin rules. Think of a battery plant in a partner country, owned by a company from a country that dominates global production. Companies offering partner content check this themselves in one standard form. A company caught twice with a false declaration within three years is excluded for one to three years. The 50% threshold is the same single-country cap the Commission already uses in the NZIA.

ev.justification: Member States should retain sufficient flexibility to design electric-vehicle support schemes around their specific market conditions, consumer purchasing power, transport needs, charging infrastructure and national decarbonisation pathways. A cost increase exceeding 20% for comparable models could place electric mobility beyond the reach of many households and businesses. This concern is particularly relevant for Malta, where households are highly dependent on private vehicles, the domestic market is small, vehicle choice may already be narrower than in larger Member States, etc. Restricting eligibility could further reduce competition, concentrate support among higher-priced vehicles and disadvantage lower- and middle-income consumers, SMEs, commercial fleets and public-service operators seeking to transition to cleaner mobility. The proposed safeguard would allow the competent authority to consider comparable vehicle prices, the availability of models across different market segments, delivery times, technical performance, charging compatibility, battery range, lifecycle costs and the expected contribution of the scheme to emissions reductions. It would also preserve technology neutrality by ensuring that support can remain open to the zero- and low-emission solutions best suited to national circumstances, rather than indirectly favouring a specific manufacturer, production location or technological configuration. The derogation would apply only where objective and transparent evidence demonstrates a material impact on affordability, consumer choice or achievement of national decarbonisation and zero-emission mobility objectives. A balanced approach would maintain incentives for European vehicle and battery production while recognising that the environmental benefits of support schemes depend primarily on the timely and broad adoption of cleaner vehicles.

ev.justification: Extending partner-origin recognition to vehicle-support schemes would ensure consistency with the broader “Made with Europe” approach established under Articles 8 and 9 and would prevent trusted partner content from being treated as automatically ineligible solely because it originates outside the Union. Modern vehicle and battery value chains are highly integrated and often depend on specialised components, critical raw materials, and other technologies sourced from reliable countries with which the Union maintains economic relations. Failing to recognise this could increase legal uncertainty for national authorities and economic operators, weaken the practical effectiveness of the partner-equivalence framework, restrict the range of eligible vehicles, reduce competition among manufacturers and importers, increase consumer prices and delay the uptake of zero- and low-emission mobility. These effects would be particularly significant for Malta, where the vehicle market is small, domestic manufacturing is absent, distribution and transport costs are comparatively high, and consumers already have access to a narrower selection of models than in larger Member States. Recognising qualifying partner content would allow support schemes to remain open to affordable and technologically suitable vehicles while maintaining incentives for Union production and investment. Eligibility should remain subject to the safeguards and criteria applicable under Articles 8 and 9. The recognition should therefore not amount to an unrestricted exemption for all third-country content, but should apply only where the partner relationship contributes to the Union’s economic security and strategic resilience.

ev.justification: The IAA should pair its requirements with incentives and additional funding that at least partially offset the increased costs of localising production, creating a genuine business case for manufacturing in the EU. At present, the most dependable incentive for cars and vans is the super-credit under the CO2 Regulation. Because it cannot be modified, cancelled, or withdrawn at Member State discretion, it offers manufacturers a degree of planning certainty the other mechanisms lack. Public support can be withdrawn by Member States or never granted in the first place. Furthermore, the proposal allows Member States to opt out of applying "Made in EU" provisions to public procurement and support schemes altogether, via the “escape clause” if it proves disproportionate costs. Effectively asking manufacturers to buy European while declining to hold public sector to the same standard. A manufacturer that has invested in local production and supply chain may see no reward for it, should a public authority simply choose to use that opt-out. Therefore, Extend the super-credit mechanism to other categories, including a super-credit of 1.3 to ALL zero-emission vehicles "Made in EU," not only small.

2a.Where the Commission has reasonable grounds to suspect, either at its own initiative or on the basis of evidence submitted by a Member State, a national type-approval authority or an association representing Union vehicle manufacturers, that manufacturing activities have been established or significantly expanded within the Union primarily for the purpose of meeting the criteria set out in Part III of Annex III, without leading to genuine economic integration into the Union’s industrial value chains, it shall open a formal investigation within 30 days of receiving such evidence or of its own decision to take action.

ev.justification: The proposed approach under the CO₂ emission performance standards does not create demand for low-carbon materials for all of the key materials needed to build a car. In particular, only steel is considered, while low-carbon aluminium is not included. This weakens policy alignment and sends a mixed signal to industry. Including low-carbon aluminium in the CO₂ credit system, alongside steel, would help ensure a more complete approach that supports the competitiveness of European value chains. This is particularly important when considering that electric vehicles tend to contain more aluminium than internal combustion engine cars (displacing steel), since aluminium is lighter than steel and lightweight EVs is crucial for improving the performance of the battery.

The Commission proposal already recognises the need to bring the chemical industry within the IAA framework. 2a.The Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts in accordance with Article 30 to supplement this Regulation as soon as possible and no later than 9 months from the entry into force of this Regulation by laying down Union-level demand-side measures, including content requirements, for zero-emission vessels and related maritime equipment, including:
(a) a minimum percentage of European content, expressed as a percentage of the total value of the vessel or maritime equipment; and
(b) a list of the strategic maritime equipment and technologies, for which EU-origin products is required as a condition for eligibility under public procurement procedures and public support schemes.
When preparing of the delegated acts, the Commission shall take into account:
(a) the contribution of the requirements to the Union’s objective of economic security, resilience and climate neutrality set out in Regulation (EU) 2021/1119;
(b) the market situation at Union level, as identified through monitoring activities, including declining Union market shares and Union industry that is producing below capacity;
(c) the impact of setting such measures on the overall competitiveness and greenhouse gas emissions of the relevant sectors, as well as on costs for downstream consumers and small and medium enterprises and public budgets.

2b.No later than 12 months after the date of entry into force of this Regulation, the Commission shall adopt a work plan for the development of the measures referred to in this paragraph, based on preparatory studies and consultation of Member States and relevant stakeholders, including industry.
The work plan shall identify the measures to be developed and, where appropriate, the end markets to be addressed. Measures implemented by delegated acts under this Article shall be limited to public procurement and public support schemes and may include amendments to Annex II in relation to the construction and automotive end markets, including the addition of product categories and the identification of chemical input materials, for which low-carbon requirements, requirements relating to the use of sustainable carbon sources, Union-origin requirements, or any combination thereof, may apply.
Measures included in the work plan shall be proportionate and may target final products, or materials, substances or mixtures incorporated in final products or end-use applications, provided that the corresponding obligations are placed on the operators placing those final products or end-use applications on the market. Such measures shall take into account the availability and implementation timelines of relevant low-carbon methodologies, and ensure coherence with relevant Union legislation, in particular Regulation (EU) 2024/3110.

ev.justification: the inclusion of a supply-adequacy check within the Article 29 review is essential as it addresses the fact that 'Made in Europe' requirements are calibrated against projected rather than existing manufacturing capacity. If EU supply of key components, most critically battery cells, fails to materialise at the scale and pace assumed, manufacturers will face binding obligations they cannot meet, driving up costs and undermining the competitiveness of EU-produced vehicles without any corresponding industrial benefit. A mandatory supply assessment at the three-year review, with the ability to adjust thresholds where shortfalls are identified, is therefore not a weakening of the Act's ambitions but a necessary safeguard to ensure those ambitions remain grounded in supply-chain reality.

ev.justification: The impact of IAA measures on energy costs should be monitored on an ongoing basis to ensure that implementation does not inadvertently raise industrial energy prices or erode the competitiveness of energy-intensive industries. Since energy companies are both regulated entities under the IAA and suppliers of energy to industrial users, energy price developments constitute an important element of the overall effectiveness assessment. Nuclear energy investments involve capital commitment horizons of 60-80 years and development cycles of 10-20 years. Subjecting nuclear-specific requirements to revision every 3 years or any short term time-frame creates regulatory instability incompatible with the investment certainty required for new nuclear builds, including SMR programmes. A 10-year review cycle is the minimum required for an adequate stable regulatory framework. In the automotive sector, given the complexity of supply chains and the pace of industrial transformation, the review should assess the actual availability, technical suitability and price competitiveness of Union-origin components. Where sufficient volumes of compliant components are not commercially available, or compliance would entail a disproportionate cost premium, appropriate flexibility should be provided to avoid undermining the competitiveness of Union manufacturers.

ev.justification: The European supply chain of inverters, power plant control, battery management systems and assembly can be ready to meet the needs of new storage systems. Given the current concentration of global battery cell production outside the EU, introducing Union-origin requirements for cells from Phase 1 under Article 26 NZIA is crucial. Early requirements prevent formal compliance loopholes, such as partial offshoring or reliance on equivalent content, ensuring genuine EU-based manufacturing capacity. Introducing cells in the initial phase also provides a timely market signal, supporting rapid BESS deployment, investor readiness, and Europe’s industrial capacity, while strengthening strategic autonomy in net-zero technologies.

(8a) In Annex II part III paragraph 1 point ca is added:
(ca)Electric charging technologies for transport: From [OP: Please insert the date = 2 years after entry into force of this Regulation], shore-side electricity supply equipment, and electric air transport supply equipment shall originate within the Union. ev.justification: Charging infrastructure should be considered an integral and indivisible part of the vehicle of the future and, consequently, of the European automotive value chain. Extending the “Made in Europe” approach and public procurement requirements to charging equipment would ensure consistency between policies supporting European vehicle manufacturing and those enabling its electrification.
